blocks.text: The macroscopic collisions are generally inelastic and do not conserve Kinetic energy.
The perfect inelastic collision is one in which the colliding objects stick together to make a single mass after collision. Its analysis can be carried out as follows:

Let us take two rigid bodies having masses m₁ and m₂ moving with velocities, v⃗₁i and v⃗₂i, respectively, in a two-dimensional xy-plane. Assume that the first body is moving along the x-axis while the second body moves in a direction, making an angle θ with x-axis. Both the bodies collide at the origin as shown in the figure 2.17.

blocks.alt: Axes x and y. Body m1 moves along the x-axis towards the origin with velocity v1i; body m2 moves towards the origin with velocity v2i along a line at angle theta to the x-axis. After colliding at the origin the combined body moves off with velocity vf at angle phi above the x-axis.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.17: Perfectly inelastic collision in two dimensions (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.17).

blocks.text: After collision, bodies stick together, having combined mass M = m₁ + m₂, which moves with velocity v⃗f, making an angle φ with x-axis. Now resolve v⃗₂i into rectangular components v⃗₂i sinθ and v⃗₂i cosθ. Also resolve v⃗f into components v⃗f sinφ and v⃗f cosφ.

blocks.text_alt: m₁v₁i cos θ₁ + m₂v₂i cos θ₂ = Mv⃗f cos φ   (2.39)
m₁v₁i sin θ₁ + m₂v₂i sin θ₂ = Mv⃗f sin φ   (2.40)
